newsitem.title: FRANCE: Europe's IT sloth could become economic drag.
newsitem.headline: Europe's IT sloth could become economic drag.

text.p: Europe's failure to match America's enthusiasm for information technology is likely to become a serious drag on economic growth, an industry expert said on Tuesday.
Less than 20 percent of European households currently own personal computers. This compares with around 35 percent in the U.S.

According to British information technology consultancy Inteco, the U.S. figure is likely to flatten out at around 50 percent, while only 35 percent of European homes will join the information superhighway by the end of the century.
This is seriously bad news for European economies, says Patrick McGovern, chairman and chief executive of IDG, the U.S. information technology consultancy and publisher.

On-line computing means more than just bored teenagers surfing the World Wide Web on rainy weekends. Computer skills and knowledge of the Internet, the worldwide network of PCs linked by telephone lines, holds the key to success in the new virtual markets of the 21st century.

And even Europeans who are excited by computers, find their stores scrammed full of U.S. brand names like International Business Machines, Compaq, Hewlett-Packard, Apple, Novell and Oracle. But on this front McGovern offers Europe some hope.

U.S. companies have hit the ground running in the race to dominate the rapidly moving markets for information technology. But the volatile nature of developments means that windows of opportunity for savvy newcomers can present themselves, while incumbents get lazy and complacent.
Delegates to IDG's "European IT Forum" here have been asssailed by proponents of the new Network Computer. Its main proselytizer here has been Larry Ellison, chairman of Oracle.

Ellison says the personal computer is too expensive and overcomplicated. His $500 Network Computer, designed to draw its brain power from the network it is connected to, will be the first device simple enough and cheap enough to become a mass market product, according to Ellison.
Unlike overpowered PCs, the Network Computer only utilises the amount of computing power needed for the task in hand.

Ellison demonstrated his new product, made by Acorn Computers of Britain and Olivetti of Italy. McGovern says this new approach to Internet access could be a golden chance for Europe to break into new high technology manufacturing.

But, meanwhile, the prospects for Europe are gloomy. Telephone costs are too high, and prices of computers are at least 25 percent higher than in the U.S. The stuttering economy is scaring away buyers.

"Europe is handicapped because telephone costs are much higher than most of the rest of the world. If this doesn't change Europe will have a serious cost disadvantage in the coming global electronic commerce," McGovern said.

"Europe has to make sure deregulation and privatisastion are really carried out vigourously. The cost to connect to the world information network in Berlin or Paris should be no different than what it is in New York or Sydney."
European Union telecommunications are due to be liberalised in 1998.

"We moving towards an information economy where a majority of world GNP will be based on ideas, designs, programmes and intellectual property being bought and sold across computer networks," McGovern said.
New, cheap devices should present Europeans with a chance.

"When the industry goes through these cycles of change as it did for mainframes to minis to PCs -- and now to network centric computing -- the well established companies are often slow to adopt to change."

"Fully half of today's top 20 IT vendors didn't exist 15 years ago. So there's a great opportunity for European companies that reinvent themselves and succeed in this new world of digital communications and electronic commerce."
